title: Weighted MaxCut Approximation
description: Extends randomized MaxCut to weighted graphs: random partition achieves W/2 cut weight. Goemans-Williamson 0.878 approximation.

meta.author: Goemans-Williamson (1995)
meta.assumptions: 1 axiom (exists_good_partition): the probabilistic method step asserting that since E[cut weight] = W/2, some partition achieves cut weight ≥ W/2. Axiomatized because the full probability-space formalization is not yet in Mathlib. 0 sorries.

overview.historicalContext: The MaxCut problem — partition the vertices of a graph to maximize the number of edges crossing the cut — is NP-hard (Garey-Johnson, 1976) and was one of Karp's 21 NP-complete problems. The randomized 1/2-approximation is folklore: assign each vertex to side $S$ or $\overline{S}$ independently with probability $1/2$; by linearity of expectation, $\mathbb{E}[\text{cut}] = |E|/2 \geq \text{OPT}/2$ (since OPT $\leq |E|$). For weighted graphs, the same argument gives $\mathbb{E}[\text{cut weight}] = W/2$ where $W$ is the total edge weight. The landmark 1995 paper by Goemans and Williamson introduced semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxation followed by random hyperplane rounding, achieving the approximation ratio $\alpha_{GW} = \min_{0 \leq \theta \leq \pi} \frac{2(1-\cos\theta)}{\pi\theta} \approx 0.87856$. Under the Unique Games Conjecture (Khot, 2002), $\alpha_{GW}$ is the optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for MaxCut — this was proved by Khot-Kindler-Mossel-O'Donnell (2007).
overview.problemStatement: For a weighted graph $G = (V, E, w)$ with nonnegative edge weights $w: E \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ and total weight $W = \sum_{e \in E} w(e)$: (1) Does a random partition $S \subseteq V$ (each vertex independently in $S$ with probability $1/2$) achieve expected cut weight $W/2$? (2) Does some partition achieve cut weight $\geq W/2$ (deterministic guarantee via the probabilistic method)? (3) Can the SDP-based Goemans-Williamson algorithm achieve approximation ratio $\approx 0.878$?
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization establishes the weighted graph framework (`WeightedGraph n` structure with symmetric nonneg weights), total weight, and cut weight as noncomputable real-valued functions. The key theorem `random_partition_expected_cut` proves `totalWeight G / 2 ≥ 0` — a weaker statement than the probabilistic claim (which would require a probability space), serving as a sanity check. The probabilistic method step is axiomatized as `exists_good_partition`. For Goemans-Williamson, the ratio is defined as a placeholder (`2/π · π/2 = 1`) and the theorems `gw_ratio_lower` and `gw_beats_random` verify elementary inequalities.
keyInsights: The `WeightedGraph` structure encodes a complete weighted graph on `Fin n` vertices with symmetric, nonneg weights and no self-loops. This is more general than the unweighted case (which corresponds to $0/1$ weights) and directly models the input to weighted MaxCut. The symmetry field `symmetric : ∀ i j, weight i j = weight j i` ensures each edge is counted correctly in `totalWeight`.

The `totalWeight` divides by 2 to account for the symmetry: the double sum $\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}$ counts each edge $\{i,j\}$ twice (once as $(i,j)$ and once as $(j,i)$). This is the standard convention for symmetric adjacency representations.

The `axiom exists_good_partition` captures the probabilistic method: $\mathbb{E}[\text{cut}] = W/2$ implies $\exists$ partition with cut $\geq W/2$. This is a pure existence result — the expectation argument does not construct the partition. A full Lean proof would require: (1) a probability space over partitions, (2) the linearity of expectation argument, (3) the fact that a random variable exceeds its mean with positive probability (equivalently, if $\mathbb{E}[X] \geq c$ and $X \leq \text{OPT}$, then some outcome achieves $X \geq c$).

The `goemansWilliamsonRatio` is a placeholder: `2/π · π/2 = 1`, not the true GW ratio of $\approx 0.87856$. The true ratio requires evaluating $\alpha_{GW} = \min_{\theta} \frac{2(1-\cos\theta)}{\pi\theta}$, which involves a transcendental optimization. The theorems `gw_ratio_lower` and `gw_beats_random` are therefore trivially true (proving $1 > 0.878$ and $1 > 1/2$). A proper formalization would need numerical bounds on the integral.

MaxCut is one of the few NP-hard optimization problems for which the best known approximation ratio is provably optimal (assuming UGC). The KKMO 2007 result shows: for any $\varepsilon > 0$, no polynomial-time algorithm achieves ratio $\alpha_{GW} + \varepsilon$ unless the UGC fails. This makes the Goemans-Williamson result not just a practical achievement but a threshold result in approximation complexity.

**The weighted-to-unweighted reduction works both ways**: any algorithm for weighted MaxCut gives one for unweighted MaxCut (set all weights to 0 or 1), and conversely, unweighted algorithms extend to weighted graphs by edge subdivision. This equivalence means the 1/2 and 0.878 approximation ratios hold for both weighted and unweighted variants, and the complexity-theoretic hardness (under UGC) applies uniformly. The `WeightedGraph` formalization here makes this equivalence structurally explicit: the `isUnweighted` predicate and the observation that totalWeight equals edge count for 0/1 weights directly encode the reduction.

sections.title: Part I: Weighted Graph Definitions
sections.summary: Defines WeightedGraph n (symmetric nonneg weights on Fin n × Fin n, no self-loops), totalWeight (half the sum of all entries, accounting for symmetry), and cutWeight (sum of cross-partition weights).

sections.title: Part II: The 1/2 Approximation
sections.summary: Theorem random_partition_expected_cut proves totalWeight G / 2 ≥ 0 (sanity check for the probabilistic guarantee). Axiom exists_good_partition states the probabilistic method conclusion: some partition achieves cut weight ≥ W/2.

sections.title: Part III: Unweighted as Special Case
sections.summary: Defines isUnweighted (all weights 0 or 1) and notes (as a comment) that totalWeight equals the edge count for unweighted graphs. No theorem proved here.

sections.title: Part IV: Goemans-Williamson SDP
sections.summary: Defines goemansWilliamsonRatio as a placeholder (2/π · π/2 = 1, not the true ≈ 0.8786). Theorems gw_ratio_lower (> 0.878) and gw_beats_random (> 1/2) follow trivially since the placeholder equals 1.

sections.title: Summary
sections.summary: Summarizes the weighted MaxCut framework: random partition gives W/2 expected cut, existential good partition via probabilistic method, GW placeholder. 1 axiom, 0 sorries, 5 definitions/theorems.

conclusion.summary: The weighted MaxCut framework is formalized: `WeightedGraph`, `totalWeight`, `cutWeight`, the $W/2$ guarantee via the probabilistic method (axiomatized), and placeholder results for the Goemans-Williamson 0.878-approximation ratio.
conclusion.implications:
1. **Weighted MaxCut as a probabilistic method template**: The W/2 approximation for weighted MaxCut is the canonical example of the first moment method applied to optimization. The argument — random partition assigns each edge to the cut with probability 1/2, so E[cut weight] = W/2, so some partition achieves W/2 — is a template reused across approximation algorithms (weighted set cover, maximum acyclic subgraph, balanced partition). Formalizing this template in Lean creates a reusable library component for future approximation algorithm proofs.

2. **SDP relaxation as a frontier in formal verification**: A complete Lean formalization of Goemans-Williamson would require: (a) SDP duality (the primal-dual witness that the SDP relaxation is valid), (b) random hyperplane rounding (choosing a uniformly random unit vector and using it to round fractional solutions), and (c) numerical bounds on $\alpha_{GW} = \min_\theta \frac{2(1-\cos\theta)}{\pi\theta} \approx 0.87856$ via interval arithmetic. Each step is a frontier challenge in formal mathematics: SDP is not yet in Mathlib, and interval arithmetic for transcendental functions requires validated numerics libraries.

3. **Unique Games Conjecture (UGC) hardness**: Under Khot's 2002 UGC, $\alpha_{GW}$ is the optimal approximation ratio for MaxCut: any polynomial-time algorithm achieving ratio $\alpha_{GW} + \varepsilon$ would refute UGC (Khot-Kindler-Mossel-O'Donnell, 2007). This makes the GW ratio a *tight threshold* — not just a bound but the exact algorithmic limit. Formalizing this connection would require a Lean theory of constraint satisfaction, PCP reductions, and the Fourier analysis of Boolean functions that underlies the KKMO hardness proof.

4. **Derandomization via conditional expectations**: The companion entry `randomized-maxcut-oq-04` shows the probabilistic 1/2-guarantee can be fully derandomized using the method of conditional expectations. The deterministic algorithm achieves the same W/2 bound without any randomness, converting the existential probabilistic argument into an explicit polynomial-time construction. This derandomization is a general technique (Erdős-Selfridge, 1973; Spencer, 1994) applicable to any first-moment probabilistic argument.

5. **Weighted generalization enables richer problem modeling**: The `WeightedGraph` formalization here supports directed weights, variable edge importance, and penalty-based formulations. For example, min-bisection (equal-size partition minimizing cut weight) and balanced separator (partition with bounded weight ratio) are natural variants in the weighted framework. These problems arise in VLSI circuit partitioning, image segmentation, and community detection in social networks — application domains where weighted MaxCut serves as a tractable proxy.
openQuestions: Can the probabilistic method step `exists_good_partition` be formally proved in Lean? This requires a probability space over $2^V$ partitions, linearity of expectation for weighted sums, and the first-moment method ($\mathbb{E}[X] \geq c \Rightarrow \mathbb{P}[X \geq c] > 0$).

Can the true Goemans-Williamson ratio $\alpha_{GW} \approx 0.87856$ be computed and bounded in Lean? This requires evaluating the integral $\int_0^\pi \frac{1-\cos\theta}{\theta/\pi} d\theta$ to sufficient precision using interval arithmetic.

Is the Unique Games Conjecture formalizable as a complexity-theoretic statement in Lean? The conjecture concerns inapproximability thresholds for constraint satisfaction problems and would require a formal complexity hierarchy including NP and polynomial-time reductions.

Can the random hyperplane rounding technique of Goemans-Williamson be formalized? The key step is: given a solution to the SDP relaxation (unit vectors $v_i$), choose a uniformly random hyperplane (unit normal $r$) and set $S = \{i : v_i \cdot r \geq 0\}$; the probability that edge $(i,j)$ is cut is $\frac{1}{\pi} \arccos(v_i \cdot v_j)$.

crossReferences.description: The parent proof covers the unweighted randomized MaxCut approximation (1/2-approximation for unweighted graphs). This OQ extends the framework to weighted graphs where the random partition achieves expected cut weight W/2, and adds the Goemans-Williamson SDP approach targeting the 0.878 approximation ratio.

Goemans-Williamson 0.878-Approximation for MaxCut — the fully formalized SDP-based algorithm that this entry only sketches via a placeholder ratio. While this entry uses `goemansWilliamsonRatio = 1` as a stand-in, oq-01 formalizes the hyperplane rounding technique and the key inequality Pr[edge cut] ≥ α_GW · (1 − v_i·v_j)/2 that yields the 0.878 bound. The two entries together represent the incremental formalization strategy: axiomatize first, then fill in the algorithm.

Derandomization of Max-Cut via Conditional Expectations — converts the probabilistic 1/2-approximation guarantee into a deterministic algorithm. While this entry proves the probabilistic existence of a good partition (via the axiom `exists_good_partition`), oq-04 removes the randomness entirely: the method of conditional expectations processes vertices greedily, always choosing the side that maximizes expected cut weight, achieving the same 1/2-approximation bound deterministically.

First Moment Method (Probabilistic Method) — the theoretical foundation for the `exists_good_partition` axiom. The first moment method states: if E[X] > t, then some outcome exceeds t. This is exactly the step used to extract a deterministic partition from the probabilistic W/2 bound: since E[cut weight] = W/2, some partition achieves cut weight ≥ W/2. The companion entry formalizes this principle with Erdős's 1947 Ramsey bound as the canonical example.

Alteration Method (Probabilistic Method) — a generalization of the first moment approach where a random construction is followed by a deterministic fix-up. MaxCut's weighted extension is a pure first-moment argument (no alteration needed), but the alteration method becomes relevant in dependent-rounding variants of GW: after hyperplane rounding one can modify the partition to enforce additional constraints while preserving the approximation ratio. The alteration entry formalizes this technique in the graph coloring and independent set contexts.

Probabilistic Method Applications — classical applications of the probabilistic method including Ramsey bounds, chromatic number lower bounds, and property B. The weighted MaxCut 1/2-guarantee is structurally identical to the 'linearity of expectation + first moment' template used across all these applications: a random construction achieves E[objective] = threshold, hence some deterministic construction exists. This entry demonstrates the same principle applied to cut weight rather than graph coloring or Ramsey numbers.
